deep.reconstruction:
This page continues a section on 'normes de Köthe' on R^(N), the finitely supported sequences. Judging from the context, these are monotone lattice norms, N(x) ≤ N(y) whenever |x| ≤ |y|, normalized so that N(e_i) = 1. On the next page they are called 'normes de Schatten', i.e. symmetric-gauge-type norms. The project is the theory of Schatten / von Neumann norm ideals (Schatten classes) for Grothendieck's tensor-product work.

The previous page extended N to arbitrary sequences by N(x) = lim_n N(|x|_n), where |x|_n is the n-th truncation of |x|. It then defined l^N = {x : N(x) < ∞}.

On this page:
(i) An inequality between two Köthe norms gives an inclusion between the corresponding l-spaces, with the identity map continuous.
(ii) Every normalized Köthe norm satisfies N_∞ = sup|x_i| ≤ N ≤ Σ|x_i| = N_1. The spaces for N_1 and N_∞ are l^1 and l^∞. Hence (6): l^1 ⊂ l^N ⊂ l^∞, with both identity injections of norm ≤ 1.
(iii) Lemma (7), countable subadditivity: N(Σ_k x^k) ≤ Σ_k N(x^k) whenever Σ N(x^k) < ∞. The proof runs as follows. By (6), Σ_k |x^k_i| < ∞, so x = Σ x^k exists coordinatewise. Then |x|_n ≤ Σ_k |x^k|_n. Since N restricted to R^n is continuous, N(Σ_k |x^k|_n) = lim_m N(Σ_{k≤m} |x^k|_n) ≤ Σ_k N(x^k). Taking sup over n gives (7).

The lemma block is enclosed and crossed with loops. The next page nevertheless uses (7) to prove that l^N is complete (a Riesz–Fischer type argument), so the block was probably moved or rewritten rather than abandoned.

In modern terms, this is the elementary theory of Banach sequence lattices with the Fatou property: the maximal symmetric sequence space of a symmetric norming function, sitting between l^1 and l^∞.
errors: The bound N_∞ ≤ N ≤ N_1 holds only for normalized norms (N(e_i) = 1). A general weighted Köthe norm does not satisfy it. The intended class is evidently normalized, i.e. symmetric gauge functions, which the next page calls 'normes de Schatten'.

The first paragraph has a direction inconsistency as written. N' ≤ N'' implies l^{N''} ⊂ l^{N'}, and the norm of l^{N''} is finer than the one induced from l^{N'}. The page appears to state the inclusion and the comparison of norms with primes swapped relative to the hypothesis. The application in (6) is correct.
Notation clash in the proof of (7): the index n is used both for the truncation |x|_n and for the partial-sum bound Σ_{k=1}^n. This is harmless.
In (7) the left side is written N(|Σ x^k|) in places. Since N(x) depends only on |x|, this is equivalent.

ideas.what: Extension of a lattice norm from finitely supported sequences to all sequences via suprema of truncations, defining the maximal space l^N
ideas.modern_name: Fatou / Lorentz–Luxemburg extension; maximal symmetric sequence space of a symmetric norming function
ideas.usually_credited_to: Köthe–Toeplitz (1934), von Neumann (1937), Schatten (1950), Lorentz, Luxemburg; Gohberg–Krein for norm ideals
ideas.where_published: Possibly related material in Produits tensoriels topologiques (1955, Mem. AMS 16), chapter on Schatten-type norms; unsure of exact presence

ideas.what: Sandwich l^1 ⊂ l^N ⊂ l^∞ (and, on the next page, l^1 ⊂ l_N ⊂ c_0) with norm-one injections
ideas.modern_name: Basic embedding of symmetric sequence spaces

ideas.what: Countable subadditivity of the extended norm, implying completeness of l^N
ideas.modern_name: Riesz–Fischer property / Fatou property implies completeness

deep.surprise_reason: This is routine foundational material on symmetric and Köthe sequence spaces, carefully worked out as groundwork for Schatten norm ideals. There is nothing beyond the standard theory.
transcription_corrections: The first paragraph probably reads 'Si N' et N'' sont deux normes de Köthe telles que N' ≤ N''…'. The subscripts '_1' and '_∞' on N', N'' in the machine transcription look like misreadings of primes or scribbles.
Margin annotations in brown ink ('R^(N)' and similar, left and right margins) are not transcribed. They seem to note that the Köthe norms live on R^(N).
The lemma block, including (7) and its proof, is struck through with large loops. It is still referenced as (7) on the next page.
